transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-12 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Maya Singh (Redwood) — Priya Patel, Marcus Liu, Dana Ortiz (Vega Retail)

Auto Summary (auto-generated): Quickstart + SDK walkthrough, auth patterns discussed, security/hosting requirements captured.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE; with me is Maya, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya Patel: Good, thanks. Excited to see the SDKs, we've been looking at integration options.
[00:12] Marcus Liu: Hi, Marcus here. We'll focus on the engineering bit — auth, env setup, and how fast we can get an end-to-end request flow.
[00:18] Dana Ortiz: And I'll be chipping in on ops/network questions — VPC, egress, that sort of thing.
[00:22] Maya Singh: Great. Today's plan: quick overview of Redwood API and Console, then a live walkthrough of the Python quickstart, a TypeScript snippet, and we'll finish with security and hosting questions.

[00:35] Alex Chen: Quick commercial note — you mentioned Dedicated capacity is interesting to you. We'll cover the tradeoffs during the call.

[01:02] Maya Singh: OK jumping into the demo — I have a local repo open. The Python SDK is deliberately small. The flow is: install package, set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env or use a service account token, then call client.generate or client.chat depending on use case.

[01:25] Marcus Liu: Is the REDWOOD_API_KEY a long-lived token? What's best practice for rotating it?

[01:29] Maya Singh: Good question. Keys can be scoped and rotated. For prod we recommend short-lived service account tokens fetched from your secrets manager and rotated via CI. For staging you can use long-lived keys with RBAC. We integrate with common KMS and secrets managers — we have examples for Vault, AWS Secrets Manager.

[01:50] Alex Chen: I'll drop the sample .env and the Vault example in the repo we send.

[02:10] Maya Singh: Here's the Python snippet —

[02:12] Maya Singh: "from redwood import RedwoodClient\nclient = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'])\nresp = client.chat.create(model='redwood-1-small', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'Summarize user feedback'}])\nprint(resp.text)"

[02:35] Priya Patel: When you call client.chat.create, does that automatically stream? We want streaming for the UI.

[02:40] Maya Singh: We support streaming — in Python you can call client.chat.stream and iterate tokens. TypeScript has built-in streaming via async iterators. We'll include a small example for React streaming.

[03:05] Marcus Liu: What about embeddings? We plan to index product reviews.

[03:10] Maya Singh: Embeddings are separate endpoints — client.embeddings.create — same auth patterns. You can batch up to N items; the SDK includes a helper that handles chunking and retry.

[03:34] Alex Chen: Quick note on costs — batching and prefix/KV cache are how we reduce per-token costs. For a high-query workload you might want Dedicated to control latency and throughput.

[03:50] Marcus Liu: Can you quantify the latency improvements on Dedicated vs hosted? Ballpark numbers?

[03:55] Maya Singh: Ballpark: hosted API latencies for small models around 80-120ms p50 for single-token early responses but it varies; Dedicated with pinned capacity and GPU pools gets you into the 30-60ms p50 range depending on model and sequence length. We'll run a benchmark with your prompt set to produce hard numbers.

[04:28] Priya Patel: For compliance we need SOC 2 and audit logs, and all keys to be customer-managed. How does Redwood handle KMS and auditing?

[04:36] Maya Singh: We support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated. We surface audit logs in the Console (per-request metadata). SOC 2 is available for hosted customers with enterprise contract; for Private you manage the control plane but we provide a compliance pack. I'll attach the SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide.

[05:02] Dana Ortiz: On VPC side, can we run Redwood Private in our VPC or do you support peering? We have strict egress policies.

[05:10] Alex Chen: Two options: Redwood Private on-prem (air-gapped) or VPC deployment. We also do VPC peering and private link for Dedicated. There are small network rules — we'll provide a checklist.

[05:30] Marcus Liu: Any gotchas for Kubernetes deployments? We run EKS with a service mesh.

[05:36] Maya Singh: We publish Helm charts and a Docker image. The main considerations are GPU drivers and kernel versions for quantized runtimes. Also make sure node GC and OOM settings are tuned; we can share best-practice manifests.

[06:02] Alex Chen: Switching to TypeScript — the flow is the same. Example:

[06:08] Alex Chen: "import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'\nconst client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })\nconst resp = await client.chat.create({ model:'redwood-1-small', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: '...' }] })"

[06:35] Priya Patel: Does the TS SDK support streaming in browser with SSE or web sockets?

[06:40] Maya Singh: We expose both; for browsers we recommend SSE or the streaming helper that upgrades to websockets for larger payloads. There's an example React hook in the repo.

[07:05] Marcus Liu: How do you handle tokenization differences across models? We have some old code that assumes a tokenization that differs.

[07:12] Maya Singh: We expose a tokenizer helper so you can measure token counts before sending. Also our Console shows token breakdown per-route so devs can debug quickly.

[07:38] Priya Patel: About rollout — if we pin model versions, can you do canary/AB rollouts?

[07:44] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, traffic shifting, and automatic fallback to a compatible model when capacity is constrained. We can show a demo of rollouts in a follow-up.

[08:02] Dana Ortiz: For the pilot, we need clear SLOs and failure modes. For example, if the model is down do you fallback to cheaper hosted variant or degrade gracefully?

[08:12] Maya Singh: Exactly — we support runtime policies: fallback by cost/latency/region. You can configure auto-fallback to a quantized or smaller model. Also can set circuit-breaker rules on error rates.

[08:35] Alex Chen: Time for a quick live code run — Maya, do you want to demo a small end-to-end request?

[08:40] Maya Singh: Sure. I'll run the Python quickstart locally — I've set REDWOOD_API_KEY in my shell.

[09:00] [screen share starts]
[09:05] Maya Singh: pip install redwood-sdk==1.4.2
[09:12] Maya Singh: exporting REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-prod-... (note: redacted in recording)
[09:20] Maya Singh: Running the script now — sending a short prompt to summarize a product review.

[09:34] Maya Singh: Response comes back and I will stream the tokens — see in console it's behaving as expected.

[09:45] Marcus Liu: Looks clean. What's the retry/backoff strategy in the SDK?

[09:50] Maya Singh: We implement exponential backoff with jitter; SDK exposes hooks to customize retries per-route. For high-throughput we recommend client-side throttling + server-side rate limits.

[10:12] Priya Patel: How do you handle PII—if user content contains PII do you have redaction or retention controls?

[10:19] Maya Singh: We surface retention settings per-tenant. For hosted you can opt-out of retention; for Dedicated/Private you control retention via policy and can integrate with DLP tooling. We also have optional response filters and PII detection hooks in the pipeline.

[10:42] Alex Chen: We should capture the pilot success criteria — Priya, what would you consider a win after the 2-week pilot?

[10:51] Priya Patel: Low-level: integrate the SDKs end-to-end in staging with streaming UI. Performance: p95 latency under 250ms for our short prompts. Business: cost estimate within project budget. Security: SOC2 attestation and KMS integration proof.

[11:15] Marcus Liu: We'll provide a traffic histogram and sample prompts; would like to run an A/B on hosted vs Dedicated if pricing looks reasonable.

[11:28] Maya Singh: Perfect. We'll run the benchmark and return a report with token-level cost and latency breakdowns.

[11:45] [small crosstalk as Alex shares next steps]

[12:02] Dana Ortiz: Regarding networking I'll check with infra — we may need private link; will confirm constraints by Friday.

[12:20] Alex Chen: For the repo — it includes Dockerfiles for both local dev and a small compose for demoing with a local secrets store. It also includes the React streaming hook and an examples/embeddings folder.

[12:38] Priya Patel: Great. A couple of questions about billing: do you meter by tokens the same for hosted and Dedicated?

[12:45] Alex Chen: Hosted is per-token. Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract with a commit and unit economics; you get lower per-token cost plus predictability. We'll outline both options in the pricing doc.

[13:05] Marcus Liu: Any limits on concurrency on Dedicated? We have spikes.

[13:10] Maya Singh: You choose GPU pool sizes and concurrency policies. Dedicated supports autoscaling with burst capacity options; exact numbers depend on the contract. We'll share sample configs for your traffic pattern.

[13:32] Priya Patel: Security doc and SOC2 — can you send the detailed pack?

[13:35] Maya Singh: Yes. I'll include SOC2 summary, SAML/SSO integration steps, KMS flow, and audit log format.

[13:50] Alex Chen: Wrapping up — recap of next steps and action owners sent to CRM.

[14:02] Priya Patel: Sounds good. Thanks Alex and Maya.

[14:05] Marcus Liu: Thanks all.

[14:07] Dana Ortiz: Thanks.

[14:10] Alex Chen: We'll follow up with the repo and docs; expect Maya's security pack and Dedicated pricing early next week.

[14:20] [meeting ends]
